What it means for customers when it ships

  • The website shows the apps as they are today rather than as they were in 2020, so what someone sees before buying is what they get.
  • A family looks the same in its app and on its page: Fire red is Fire red in both places, EMS green is EMS green.
  • Every screen in every app takes its colour from that app's record, so a colour set in the admin panel reaches the whole app instead of most of it.
  • The two open decisions can be made from evidence: the colours are written down, and every change is shown side by side.

None of this reaches a customer until it is pushed, merged and, for the server, promoted. Today nothing is merged.

U1 · One colour set per product family: what the theme fix does

Each app already paints itself from its bundle record on the server, and the website's product pages read each product record. Those records disagreed with themselves: the Fire app's primary is red but its products said blue; the EMT bundle's link text was cerulean while everything else used grey; five products carried the all-cerulean default; one had a pink background. The fix gives every family one eight-value set, built only from colours it already has, and writes it into both stores. No family's primary moves: Fire stays #D60000, EMS stays #008000, Interview stays #33C3FF, so nothing customers hold in their hands changes colour except one thing: the EMS and Interview apps' small row-description text goes from cerulean to the grey the Fire app already uses.

One question for you. Keep the EMS primary at the live #008000 (what the shipped app shows today; the default here), or move it to the register's proposed #1F6B36 (the darker green the EMT and EMR web pages show today)? Keep = the two EMS web pages go #008000; move = the whole EMS app re-tints on its next open, no store build. It is one constant either way.
Familyprimaryaccentbuttonbackgroundtext_linkstext · headings · sub_headings
Fire (bundle 6, 14 products)#D60000#D96565#085ABA → #D60000#33C3FF#8E9CB8#000000
EMS (bundle 11, 3 products + NREMT-B)#008000#7BA389#33C3FF → #008000#33C3FF#33C3FF → #8E9CB8#000000
Interview (bundle 12, 1 product)#33C3FF#33C3FF#33C3FF#33C3FF#33C3FF → #8E9CB8#000000

The full record-by-record table (3 bundles, 19 products, before → after) is docs/brand/theme-fix-2026-08.md on the server branch. It is applied by a reversible data migration that runs on the next server promotion, or by hand in the admin from the same table if you prefer that.

U3 · The apps: the store listing against the app as it runs today

Two different things are on show here, and only one of them is ours. Left is the picture the website has been showing: the app store listing screenshot. Right is the same screen from the app as it runs today, built from its own product branch and photographed in the simulator this evening. That is a store listing against a live app, not a before and after of this session: the differences between the two columns were introduced by earlier work in 2023 and 2024, traced under U5. Fire's listing is from 2020 and blue; EMS's is green but shows the old typeface, tab bar and Skip button; only the Interview listing (June 2026) matches the app that ships today, which is why its three files stay and only the six Fire and EMS files are replaced. The app change is open as four pull requests, one per product branch, and is not visible in these pictures at all: it makes the last few screens read their colours from the bundle record like the rest of the app, and every screen shown here already did. The one colour that does move between the two columns of the EMS and Interview rows, the small row description text going from cerulean to the grey the Fire app already shows, comes from the theme fix on the server, not from the app change: the migration writes #8E9CB8 into that bundle's link-text value and the row has always read the bundle theme. All three apps were built from their own branches and run in the iPhone simulator. For the signed-in screens they were pointed at a local copy of the backend seeded from the live API's own public data with one subscribed test customer, so results and build a quiz carry real attempts and real chapters; nothing was written to production. The full capture record, every raw simulator image in order, is its own page.

U5 · Why today's app does not look like its store listing

Asked and traced in the code this evening, because the right-hand column reads as a step backwards from the left. Three separate changes, all made before this year's work, none of them from this session. Each one is a commit anyone can open.

What you seeCauseWhenWhat it would take to undo
The typeface is thinner and wider. The listing shows the bold condensed brand face; the app today shows the iPhone system font.The four Trade Gothic files were registered in the iOS app at the start (9c591d4, the original project). They were dropped from the registration when the iOS target was migrated and then renamed (11bc485, 8064802). The font files still ship and 140 style rules still ask for them, so iOS has been quietly substituting its own font ever since. Android still loads them, so the two platforms have not matched since 2023.31 July and 5 September 2023Re-register the four files in the iOS app and rebuild. No design work, no server change; it needs a store release to reach customers.
Course titles are grey rather than black.The course card title colour was set to the built-in dark grey #808080 (15897f2, and its sibling 28ae6c1 on the EMT branch). It is written into the app, not into the admin panel, so no colour setting can change it and the theme fix does not touch it.6 February 2024One line per branch, then a store release.
On quiz screens the coloured header bar stops short of the right edge, leaving a notch.Every screen's header title is set 140 points narrower than the window, in the original 2020 code and copied into ten screens. It was invisible while the condensed font kept the title on one line inside the navigation bar; with the substituted font the second line drops below the bar, and the short band shows against the page.Original code, 2020; visible since the font substitutionFixing the font registration is likely to hide it again. Worth re-checking on a rebuilt app before touching the layout.
The bottom bar has two tabs where the listing shows three.The Progress tab was removed deliberately because it was crashing (e04cc7e and its two siblings).11 July 2026Nothing to undo. The listing is simply older than the app.

None of these are the theme fix or the app change in this session, and none are on a branch here. They are named so the store screenshot refresh (Asana 1217584349769767) is not taken on an app that still substitutes its own font: the fix is small, and the screenshots are worth more once it is in.

U4 · How this was checked

  • The migration was run on a local copy of the production database engine (MySQL 5.6) seeded with the exact live records: forward writes every after value for 3 bundles and 19 products; backward restores every before value; forward again changes nothing more; empty and oddly-keyed records handled; a missing record is skipped. Nothing about the API's shape changes, only values inside the colour settings.
  • The app change is small: six files (seven on the EMT branch, five on the older interview branch) that still read the built-in palette now read the bundle theme like the other sixty-two. Lint on those files: one more instance of a warning the code base already carries in every style file of this kind; no new kind of problem. All three apps were built from their product branches with Xcode 26 and ran in the iOS 26.1 simulator with the change in place, signed out against the live API and signed in against the seeded local one; libraries, course pages, quizzes, results and build a quiz rendered from each bundle theme as before.
  • Independent review: Codex could not run before the push. Every attempt on all seven branches stopped at its usage limit (“try again at Aug 20th, 2026 11:05 AM”), and the branches were pushed on 18 August on the founder's instruction. An independent Claude review ran the same evening in its place, separate from the agent that wrote the work, over five lanes at once (the migration, the app change, the restyle, the register, and these pages), with a second agent set to refute each finding before it counted. Nine findings survived, all inside the pull requests: three in the migration (a colour record that is not a key-value map is now replaced instead of stopping the run, the rewritten keys keep the spelling the apps read, and the EMT primary is one named constant), one in the website learnings note (the homepage caches the product list for 600 seconds, not never), and five in the register. All nine were fixed and pushed that night; the migration was then re-proved forward, backward and forward again on the local database rig, and the app change and the server logo pull request came back clean. Codex still makes its own pass when the limit resets on 20 August, and anything it finds lands as further commits on the same pull requests, before any merge.

Kept below unchanged for the record. Everything above is the later work.

01The logo

The old mark was a shield outline with a serif "3" typed in Georgia. It depended on whatever font the device had and read as clip art. The new mark is drawn as pure geometry: a bold gold Maltese cross faceted like an enamel badge, and a numeral 3 drawn as a shape. It reads at 16px in a browser tab and holds at 1024px as an app icon. Two versions to choose from, same colours: A on a plain navy tile, or D inside the shield outline from the previous mark.

What the mark means

The Maltese cross is the fire service's own emblem, worn on helmets and badges for over a century; its eight points are traditionally read as the firefighter's virtues. The 3 is Code 3: the radio call for lights and sirens, an emergency response, and the name of the company. Navy is the uniform; gold is the badge and the insignia. The arms are cut into two planes, lit from top-left, so the cross reads as a piece of insignia rather than a flat icon. The shield (version D) is protection and rank, carried over from the previous mark; version A drops it for a cleaner tile that sits naturally as an app icon and a browser-tab favicon.

At every size it is actually used
